items.prompt: A function classifies signed integers as prime or not prime. Which boundary rule is correct?
constraints: Prime means a positive integer with exactly two positive divisors.

options.text: Every n<2 is not prime; 2 is the smallest prime.
1 is prime because it is divisible by itself.
A negative integer is prime whenever its absolute value is prime.
0 is prime because every integer divides it.

feedback.reason: The prime domain begins at 2; zero, one, and negative integers do not have exactly two positive divisors.

blocks.text: The number 1 has only one positive divisor, while zero has infinitely many divisors in the divisibility sense. Standard prime factorization treats a negative sign separately from the prime factors of the magnitude, but the negative integer itself is not called prime. Handling n<2 before a divisor loop prevents empty-loop logic from accidentally labelling 0 or 1 as prime.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.one_is_prime: One has only one positive divisor, so it fails the defining two-divisor contract.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.negative_abs_prime: The magnitude may have prime factors, but the signed negative integer is outside the standard positive-prime domain.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.zero_prime: Having many divisors is not the same as having exactly two; zero is not prime.

items.prompt: For nonnegative signed 64-bit n and positive candidate divisor d, which trial-division condition checks d <= sqrt(n) without overflow or floating rounding?
constraints: The exact-square divisor must be tested.

options.text: d <= n / d
d*d <= n in signed 64-bit
d <= (long long)sqrt((double)n)
d < n / d

feedback.reason: The quotient condition is mathematically equivalent in the positive domain and preserves the exact-square boundary.

blocks.text: If n has a composite factorization, at least one factor is at most sqrt(n). Testing through d<=n/d therefore suffices and avoids the potentially overflowing product d*d. The non-strict comparison includes n=d*d. Floating sqrt may round at the boundary, especially near large integers. The preconditions n≥0 and d>0 are essential; division by zero or uncontrolled signs would invalidate the rewrite.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.d_squared_le_n: The product can overflow before it is compared with n.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.d_le_sqrt_double: The floating square root can round below an exact integer factor and is unnecessary.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.d_lt_n_div_d: The strict relation skips an exact square factor at d*d=n.

items.prompt: Order the steps for trial-dividing a positive integer n into prime factors with multiplicity.
constraints: The loop guard must avoid p*p overflow.

elements.text: Initialize an empty factor list or exponent map and set p to the first candidate.
While p <= n/p, test the current candidate.
While n % p == 0, record p and replace n by n/p.
Advance p to the next candidate after all copies of the current factor are removed.
After the loop, if n>1, record n as the final prime factor.

feedback.reason: All copies of a factor must be removed before the candidate advances, and a leftover greater than one is appended only after the square-root bound has been exhausted.

blocks.text: Maintain the invariant that the factors already recorded, multiplied by the current working n, equal the original input. Repeated division records multiplicity and shrinks n, which also tightens the divisor bound.

items: Initialize the factor result and start with candidate p = 2.
For n = 84, the guard 2 <= 84/2 holds. Divide by 2 repeatedly, recording 2 twice and leaving n = 21.
Advance to p = 3. The guard holds; record 3 once and leave n = 7.
Advance after exhausting 3. No later candidate satisfies p <= 7/p, so the loop ends.
Because n = 7 > 1, append 7 once. The recorded product 2·2·3·7 reconstructs 84.

blocks.title: Factorization invariant
blocks.text: Remove every copy of p before advancing, and append a leftover greater than one only after the divisor bound fails. That leftover must be prime: a composite remainder would have a factor at most its square root and the loop would not have finished.

items.prompt: Trial division has removed every factor p while p <= n/p. The remaining n is 37. What must the algorithm do?
constraints: All earlier candidate factors were fully removed.

options.text: Append 37 once as a prime factor.
Discard it because the loop has already passed sqrt(n).
Divide 37 by the last tested p in floating point and round the result.
Append both 1 and 37 as prime factors.

feedback.reason: A leftover greater than one after exhaustive trial division is prime and must be included exactly once.

blocks.text: If the remaining n were composite, it would have a factor at most its square root, and that factor would have been tested before the loop ended. Because all copies of earlier candidates were removed, the leftover 37 is a single prime factor. One is never a prime factor, and floating ratios add no divisibility evidence. This rule is especially important when the original number contains one large prime factor.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.discard_37: Discarding the leftover loses a valid prime factor that was too large to appear as the smaller member of a tested pair.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.factor_by_floating_ratio: Exact factorization depends on divisibility, not a rounded quotient.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.append_1_and_37: One is the multiplicative identity, not a prime factor.

items.prompt: In a sieve of Eratosthenes for integers up to N, p is currently known prime. Where should marking of new multiples of p begin?
constraints: Products are evaluated in a type that can represent the index.
The outer loop runs only while p <= N/p.

options.text: Begin at p*p, because smaller multiples of p already have a smaller prime factor.
Always begin at 2*p because no smaller multiple can have been marked.
Begin at p and mark the prime itself composite.
Begin at floor(sqrt(p)) because that is the first possible factor.

feedback.reason: Every composite multiple kp with k

blocks.text: Starting at p*p avoids redundant work while preserving correctness. The outer guard p<=N/p prevents forming p*p when it would exceed N and helps avoid overflow; the actual multiplication still must use a safe index type. Starting at 2p is correct but needlessly repeats marks, while starting at p destroys the prime classification. This boundary transfers to segmented sieves, where the first multiple in a segment is max(p*p, ceil(L/p)*p).

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.start_two_p: It remains correct but repeats work for multiples already handled by smaller prime factors, so it misses the decisive sieve invariant.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.start_p: That marks p itself composite even though p is known prime.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.start_sqrt_p: sqrt(p) is not generally a multiple of p and has no role as a marking index.

items.prompt: You must answer 200,000 primality queries, and every queried value lies in [0,10^7]. Which approach best matches the workload?
constraints: Memory for a boolean table through 10^7 is available.
All queries are known to share the same upper bound.

options.text: Build one sieve through 10^7, then answer each query by table lookup.
Trial-divide every queried value independently up to its square root.
Cache floating square roots and classify numbers by exact equality with their rounded roots.
Compute gcd(value,10^7) and call the value prime when the gcd is 1.

feedback.reason: A shared bounded query domain makes one preprocessing pass reusable across a large number of lookups.

blocks.text: The sieve pays roughly O(N log log N) once and then answers each query in O(1). Independent trial division repeats work up to sqrt(value) for every query. Gcd with the upper bound does not characterize primality, and floating square roots only detect perfect squares, not general composites. The decision boundary changes for one or a few very large values or when the table memory is unavailable.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.trial_divide_each: It is correct with a proper boundary but wastes the shared bounded domain by repeating factor tests across 200,000 queries.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.float_sqrt_cache: A number can be composite without being a perfect square, and floating equality is not a primality test.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.gcd_with_upper_bound: Being coprime to 10^7 does not imply being prime; many composite values satisfy that gcd.

items.prompt: Classify the standard sieve of Eratosthenes that stores a boolean composite table for all integers 0..N and marks multiples from p*p.
constraints: The table is not bit-compressed for the asymptotic classification.

feedback.reason: The harmonic contribution over prime multiples yields O(N log log N) marking work, and the table stores one state per integer.

blocks.text: For each prime p, the sieve marks about N/p multiples. Summing 1/p over primes up to N grows like log log N, giving O(N log log N) total work for the standard analysis. The boolean table covers N+1 indices, so extra space is O(N). A segmented sieve changes the working-memory boundary but not the basic factor-marking invariant.

items.prompt: Which statement correctly classifies 0 and 1 for ordinary integer primality?

options.text: Neither is prime: primes are integers greater than 1 with exactly two positive divisors.
1 is prime because it divides itself and every number has at least one divisor.
0 is prime because every nonzero integer divides it.
Both are prime as the smallest nonnegative integers.

feedback.reason: The prime definition starts at 2 and requires exactly two positive divisors.

blocks.text: One has only one positive divisor, and zero has infinitely many divisors rather than exactly two. Boundary checks for n<2 should precede trial division or sieve logic.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.one_prime: 1 does not have two distinct positive divisors.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.zero_prime: Zero has more than two divisors and is outside the prime domain.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.both_prime: Being small and nonnegative is not the primality definition.

items.prompt: During trial division, all candidate factors p have been tested through p <= n/p, and the remaining n is greater than 1. What can be concluded?

options.text: The remaining n is prime and should be emitted once as the final factor.
The remaining n is composite because no smaller factor was found.
Discard it because all factors must have been removed in pairs.
Restart trial division from 2 because the divisor bound was inconclusive.

feedback.reason: A composite remaining factor would have a factor at most its square root, which the loop already tested.

blocks.text: After removing all small factors, any remaining n>1 has no divisor up to sqrt(n), so it is prime. It may be a large prime factor with multiplicity one. Dropping it makes the factorization incomplete.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.leftover_always_composite: A composite integer must have a factor at most its square root.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.discard_leftover: The remaining prime is part of the factorization.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.restart_from_two: The divisor-bound proof already establishes primality of the leftover.

items.prompt: A sieve stores primality only for odd numbers greater than 2. Which initialization and marking rule preserves correctness?

options.text: Treat 2 as prime separately, initialize odd candidates as prime, and mark odd multiples of each discovered odd p from p*p.
Ignore 2 because an odd-only sieve cannot represent even primes.
For every p, start marking at 2p even when evens are not stored.
Leave every odd candidate true because odd numbers cannot be composite.

feedback.reason: Odd-only storage is valid only when the special prime 2 and the reduced multiple domain are handled explicitly.

blocks.text: Composite odd numbers have odd prime factors, so marking their odd multiples from p² is sufficient. Even multiples need not be stored, but 2 must remain queryable as a prime. Starting below p² repeats work already implied by smaller factors.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.drop_two: 2 is prime and remains part of the requested domain even if it is stored separately.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.mark_from_two_p: The reduced representation does not store even multiples, and starting at 2p adds redundant work.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.all_true_no_mark: Odd composites such as 9 and 15 still need to be marked.

constraints: Prime means having exactly two positive divisors.

options.text: 1 has only one positive divisor, itself, so it does not meet the exactly-two-divisor definition.
options.explanation: The prime definition excludes one by divisor count.

options.text: 1 is not prime because primes must be greater than 2.
options.explanation: The reason is the divisor definition, not a universal lower threshold of 3.

options.text: 1 is composite because it has more than two divisors.
options.explanation: 1 is neither prime nor composite under the standard classification.

options.text: 1 is not prime because it is even.

feedback.reason: The classification of 1 is a base case for primality logic and factorization.

blocks.text: A primality loop that starts from 2 must handle n<2 explicitly. Treating 1 as prime corrupts sieve counts and factor lists.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.too_large: The reason is the divisor definition, not a universal lower threshold of 3.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.composite: 1 is neither prime nor composite under the standard classification.

items.prompt: Why is testing divisors only through floor(sqrt(n)) sufficient for primality of n>1?
constraints: If n is composite, it has a factor pair greater than one.

options.text: If both factors exceeded sqrt(n), their product would exceed n; therefore a composite n has a factor at or below sqrt(n).
options.explanation: One member of every nontrivial factor pair is small enough to test.

options.text: All composite numbers are perfect squares, so sqrt is the only divisor needed.
options.explanation: Composites can have unequal factor pairs.

options.text: Factors above sqrt never exist for composites.
options.explanation: They can exist as the partner of a small factor.

options.text: sqrt(n) tests are logarithmic because square root grows like log n.
options.explanation: The numeric bound is O(sqrt n), not O(log n).

feedback.reason: The square-root bound follows from the structure of factor pairs, not from a logarithmic complexity claim.

blocks.text: If no divisor up to sqrt(n) exists, no nontrivial factor pair can exist. Testing beyond the bound repeats the partner factors unnecessarily.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.prime_square: Composites can have unequal factor pairs.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.larger_factors_irrelevant: They can exist as the partner of a small factor.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.log_bound: The numeric bound is O(sqrt n), not O(log n).

constraints: All smaller multiples of p have already been considered.

options.text: Any multiple p*q with q

options.text: Multiples below p*p are never divisible by p.

options.text: Only p itself is a multiple relevant to primality; p*p begins composite values.
options.explanation: All multiples matter, but earlier ones are already handled.

options.text: Starting at p*p makes the sieve logarithmic in the number of primes.
options.explanation: The optimization is about avoiding duplicate marking, not changing the main bound that way.

feedback.reason: The sieve avoids redundant work because composite multiples below p² have a smaller prime factor.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.skip_valid_multiples: They are divisible by p but already marked by smaller factors.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.p_prime_only: All multiples matter, but earlier ones are already handled.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sqrt_not_needed: The optimization is about avoiding duplicate marking, not changing the main bound that way.

items.prompt: After trial-dividing n by all primes up to sqrt of the remaining value, what can an unremoved remainder greater than one represent?
constraints: All possible smaller prime factors were removed.

options.text: The remainder itself is prime, because a composite remainder would have a factor at or below its square root and thus below the tested bound.
options.explanation: The leftover factor is the final prime factor with its remaining multiplicity.

options.text: It must be composite because all small factors were removed.
options.explanation: A remaining prime factor is expected.

options.text: Discard it because factorization is complete once trial division stops.
options.explanation: Discarding loses a prime factor larger than the tested divisors.

options.text: It can only be a perfect square of the last tested prime.
options.explanation: A leftover may be any prime value.

feedback.reason: Trial division leaves at most one prime factor larger than the current square-root frontier.

blocks.text: The remaining value can be appended to the factorization once, or with its multiplicity if the loop maintains the proper bound. Ignoring it yields an incomplete factorization.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.always_composite: A remaining prime factor is expected.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.ignore: Discarding loses a prime factor larger than the tested divisors.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.square_only: A leftover may be any prime value.
